posts.copy:
Ten years of duplicated housing costs can still be visible half a century later.

In a GreyScienx lifetime model, two otherwise identical Gauteng couples each bring home R50,000 a month: one partner R30,000, the other R20,000. Both stay together from 25 to 75, raise the same children and, where the scenario allows, buy the same home. The difference: one couple combines households at 25; the other keeps two homes until 35.

Under the central assumptions, sharing one home releases R8,500 a month at 25. By 35, the Early household has R2.260m in combined net worth, including pension saving, versus R1.072m for the Later household — a R1.188m head start.

From 35 onward, their housing arrangement and modeled shocks are identical. But their balance sheets are not. The earlier saving keeps compounding, while a smaller buffer leaves the Later household more exposed to expensive negative balances.

At 75, the model puts combined household wealth at R13.833m for the Early couple and R9.861m for the Later couple: a R3.972m gap in constant 2026 rand.

The result survives across three scenarios. The age-75 advantage ranges from about R1.9m in the adverse case to R11.3m in the favourable case. That range is not a forecast. It is a counterfactual under stated assumptions, including that available surplus is invested.

Nor is this a claim that people should move in together for money, or that each partner owns half. Separate homes can buy privacy, independence, safety and time to test compatibility. Relationship costs and bargaining power can erase or reverse the financial gain.

The narrower finding is harder to dismiss: household formation has a balance-sheet effect. The direct saving matters; the larger force is time — decades of compounding and protection from deficits.

Read the full paper:
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Scenario bar chart headed ‘Ten years of shared housing leaves the household ahead at 75.’ Three horizontal bars show the modeled age-75 advantage of moving in at 25 rather than 35: best case R11.287 million, average case R3.972 million, and worst case R1.882 million. Values are combined household outcomes in constant 2026 rand; the worst-case figure is a smaller funding shortfall, not positive wealth.

posts.copy:
Central Gauteng model: two homes cost R44,800 a month; one shared home costs R36,300. The R8,500 gap—not higher income—creates the head start. Constant 2026 rand.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Before-and-after horizontal bar chart comparing monthly household cost at age 25 in the average scenario. Two separate homes cost R44,800; one shared home costs R36,300; the difference is R8,500 per month. Values are constant 2026 rand in a hypothetical Gauteng model.

posts.copy:
Central model: the Early household leads by R1.188m at 35. Living arrangements then match, but the gap compounds to R3.972m by 75. Timing becomes capital. Constant 2026 rand.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Two horizontal bars compare the Early household’s modelled lead in the average scenario: R1.188 million at age 35 and R3.972 million at age 75. The bars show how the initial balance-sheet lead grows after both couples have the same living arrangement. Values are constant 2026 rand.

posts.copy:
Worst-case model: both households end with funding shortfalls. Moving in at 25 leaves the age-75 shortfall R1.882m smaller, but does not fix retirement. A buffer, not a cure.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Number-front card showing R1.882 million, the amount by which the Early household’s age-75 funding shortfall is smaller in the worst-case model. The Early path ends at negative R16.346 million and the Later path at negative R18.228 million in constant 2026 rand. These are unfunded lifestyle gaps, not literal lender debt.

posts.copy:
Best-case model: R1.261m of living costs avoided becomes an R11.287m age-75 wealth lead as early savings earn returns. A favourable scenario, not a promise. Constant 2026 rand.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Two horizontal bars compare R1.261 million in lifetime living costs avoided with an R11.287 million age-75 combined household wealth lead in the best-case model. The larger bar illustrates the effect of decades of compounding. Values are constant 2026 rand and represent a favourable scenario, not a forecast.

posts.copy:
Combined household wealth is not a 50/50 ownership statement. The model tracks one balance sheet—not who owns the assets, controls the money or performs unpaid work.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Fine-print card displaying the large word ‘UNEQUAL’ beneath the headline ‘Household wealth is not 50/50.’ It explains that combined household wealth does not prove equal control and that ownership and unpaid work require separate ledgers.

posts.copy:
The model does not say moving in early is always better. Separate homes can buy privacy, independence, safety and time to test compatibility—benefits the financial ledger cannot price.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Fine-print card headed ‘Separate homes can buy more than space,’ with the large word ‘UNPRICED.’ It lists privacy, independence, safety and time to test compatibility as real benefits omitted from the financial model.

posts.copy:
One rent avoided can improve household finances while measured consumption falls. GDP does not count an avoided transaction as output. That is the welfare–GDP paradox.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Concept card showing ‘GDP’ with a downward arrow beneath the headline ‘A household can spend less and be better off.’ It explains that an avoided second rent improves the household balance sheet but is not counted as new economic output.

posts.copy:
Housing demand depends on household formation, not population alone. For ten years, the model’s Later couple supports two homes while the Early couple supports one.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Mechanism card showing ‘2 to 1’ for the number of homes maintained during the model’s first ten years: two homes for the Later couple versus one for the Early couple. It links household formation to housing and infrastructure demand.

posts.copy:
The modelled advantage can reverse if sharing barely cuts costs, the saving is spent, career costs are large, or separation costs exceed the benefit.
https://greyscienx.com/research/household-economics/greyscienx-economics-of-living-together.pdf
posts.alt: Fine-print card displaying a large ‘IF’ beneath the headline ‘The result can reverse.’ It says savings must survive real life and that small savings or consumed surplus can erase the advantage.
